newsitem.title: CANADA: Ethyl sues Canada for $250 mln over MMT ban.
newsitem.headline: Ethyl sues Canada for $250 mln over MMT ban.

text.p: Ethyl Corp said on Monday it filed a claim against Canada for at least US$250 million for the government's legislation to shut its gasoline additive MMT out of the Canadian market.

"Ethyl Corporation has filed a claim for compensation under the North American Free Trade Agreement for not less than US$250 million (C$345 million) against the Government of Canada," it said in a statement.
It charged that the government breached its obligations under NAFTA "for harm done to its subsidiary Ethyl Canada."

Ethyl, which is the only supplier of MMT to the Canadian market, said the impetus was last week's passage by the Senate of Bill C-29, a measure that had already passed Parliament's other chamber, the House of Commons.
That bill, which must still receive routine royal assent before becoming law, would ban the import and inteprovincial trade of MMT, methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl.
MMT has been used in Canada since 1977 to replace lead in boosting octane in gasoline.

Ethyl said it increased the efficiency of gasoline production and cut nitrogen oxide emissions. But environmentalists said it was potentially a hazard and automakers said it gummed up cars' diagnostic systems and could therefore lead to more pollution. Opponents of the bill asked for proof of these assertions.

Ethyl said this was the first time a NAFTA investor used the NAFTA to file a claim against Canada seeking compensation for damages caused by legislation, and the first to involve what it said was the government's expropriation of property.
The company had filed a notice of intent to submit the NAFTA claim on September 10, though it had previously used a figure of US$200 million.
Chris Hicks, Ethyl Canada's vice president for government relations, said the government had failed to act during the 90-day consultation period which follows an intent notice.

"We were extremely disappointed in the government's refusal to consult. Now that the bill has been passed by the Senate, the government has given us no choice but to seek compensation. The bill is aimed at Ethyl as the sole producer of MMT," Hicks said.

One of Ethyl's arguments centers on the fact that MMT is not banned, just that it cannot cross national or provincial boundaries. Governments can ban substances, the argument runs, but if just the cross-border trade in them is banned, it would appear to discriminate against firms such as Ethyl engaged in such trade.

The company said the government department Health Canada had stated that MMT did not represented a health risk, and Environment Canada had admitted it could not prohibit MMT under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
Environment Minister Sergio Marchi has countered that banning imports and interprovincial trade was a normal way Canada used to curb various commodities.

Ethyl Canada President David Wilson commented: "The government can pass any legislation it wants, but when your business is taken away from you, there has to be compensation. That is what the NAFTA intends."
The statement said the issuance of the claim would lead to the creation of an arbitration panel, and it was expected there would be a hearing and decision in 1997.
